messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi was a 26-year-old South Asian man who had been married less than a year and worked as an editor, often late into the evening in a quiet office where he could lose himself in copy and avoid being alone with his thoughts. His symptoms began after a police encounter in his early twenties, when he was stopped, questioned for hours, and manhandled in a holding room that smelled of sweat, disinfectant, and stale metal. He remembered standing with his wrists twisted behind him in a position that left his shoulders aching, the harsh air on his skin, and the helplessness of being surrounded by officers who treated his fear as insolence. What had made that night stick was not only the humiliation but the sense that he had no way to explain himself or make it stop.

In the months afterward, certain moments in ordinary life began to feel loaded with danger. If his skin was suddenly hit by a particular temperature—cold air from a fan, a chill surface in a room, even a splash of water he had not expected—Ravi would go tight inside and immediately judge himself for falling apart over something so small. He had come to believe his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper, and that belief hardened quickly into the thought that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The same thing happened when he found himself alone with women, even in innocent situations such as chatting with a female colleague in the office hallway or being left in a room with his wife’s cousin at family gatherings; he would feel exposed and strangely watched, as if any interaction could go wrong and confirm that he was not capable of handling his own life. At work, he noticed that the sight of his editor’s desk, the office hum, and even a sudden draft across his forearms could leave him unsettled and self-critical, and he started arranging his day so he would not be caught off guard.

Once those beliefs took hold, the memories grew sharper and more intrusive. When the event came to mind, Ravi did not just remember it as a story; he felt overwhelming grief rise in his chest, and the memory seemed to pull his body back into the same position it had been in that room, shoulders pulled back, arms held awkwardly, jaw clenched. Sometimes the memory arrived with a smell he could not place for a second but knew belonged to that night, and the combination of the odor and the bodily sensation made him feel that the humiliation was happening again rather than being remembered. Afterward he would sink into the thought that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. He had once taken pride in his work, in sending polished pages to print and in building a home with his wife, but now those things felt thin and distant, as if the event had emptied them of value.

That grief and those memories also fed the very situations he feared most. After a vivid recollection, Ravi became more alert to temperature changes and to whether women were nearby, scanning rooms before entering them and feeling a jolt of dread if he realized he might be left alone with a woman in an office meeting or at a family visit. The moment he began to feel detached or unreal, he took that as proof that he was not in control, and the thought that he was a poor coper returned with force. He then avoided small practical risks that had become tied to the memory: he asked colleagues to keep doors open, arranged to work from home more often, and would leave social gatherings early if he thought he might be left in a one-to-one conversation with a woman. Those choices brought brief relief, but they also narrowed his life; he became less present with his wife, less willing to attend family events, and increasingly isolated in the very routines he had tried to preserve.

By the time he sought help, Ravi was tired of living in this shrinking circle. He described feeling trapped between the grief that rushed in when he remembered the night with police and the self-contempt that followed every bad moment, each feeding the other until even a cold room or a brief pause alone with a woman could set the whole sequence in motion. He came to treatment because he was afraid that if this continued, he would lose not only his confidence but the meaning he had once found in his work and marriage, and he was hoping for a way to feel like himself again without bracing for the next reminder.
